title: Jackson Financial's Third-Quarter Adjusted Operating Earnings Rise to $517 Million as Record RILA Sales of $3.0 Billion Lift Retail Annuity Sales 22%
summary: Jackson Financial reported third-quarter 2026 net income to common shareholders of $847 million ($12.37 per diluted share), adjusted operating earnings of $517 million ($7.55 per share), record registered index-linked annuity sales of $3.0 billion and a $1 billion increase in its buyback authorization.
description:
Jackson Financial Inc., the parent of Jackson National Life Insurance Company, has reported its third-quarter 2026 results. The company sells variable annuities, registered index-linked annuities (RILAs), fixed and fixed index annuities, and institutional products, and it manages assets through PPM America. The figures below come from the earnings release Jackson filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission as Exhibit 99.1. Where this article adds a percentage or a difference, it is calculated here from the reported figures and is labelled as such.

The headline numbers

Net income attributable to common shareholders was $847 million, or $12.37 per diluted share, compared with $65 million, or $0.92 per diluted share, in the third quarter of 2025. That is a very large swing, and it is mostly an accounting effect rather than a sign that the underlying business grew thirteen-fold. Jackson hedges the guarantees in its variable annuities, and under U.S. GAAP the hedging instruments and the liabilities they protect are marked to market in different places on the income statement. The release shows net losses on hedging instruments of $1,682 million, offset by gains of $1,071 million on market risk benefits, and net hedging results classified as non-operating of negative $213 million. The release also reports a gain of $337 million from business reinsured to third parties, against a loss of $176 million a year earlier. Those items sit outside Jackson's own measure of operating performance.

The measure the company emphasises is adjusted operating earnings, which strips out those hedging and reinsurance effects. On that basis Jackson earned $517 million, or $7.55 per diluted share, against $433 million, or $6.16, a year earlier. Calculated here, that is growth of about 19% in total dollars and about 23% per share, and the faster per-share growth reflects the smaller share count after buybacks. Excluding what Jackson calls notable items, adjusted operating earnings were $7.67 per diluted share against $5.98. Pretax adjusted operating earnings, which sum the four reporting segments, were $612 million against $505 million, or roughly 21% higher by the same calculation.

Where the earnings came from

The Retail Annuities segment did nearly all of the work. Its pretax adjusted operating earnings were $638 million, against $494 million a year earlier, an increase of about 29% calculated here. The Institutional Products segment earned $23 million against $31 million. The Closed Life and Annuity Blocks segment, which holds older business no longer being sold, lost $3 million against a profit of $15 million. The Corporate and Other segment lost $46 million against a loss of $35 million. Added together, $638 million plus $23 million, less $3 million and $46 million, gives the $612 million total, which matches the prior-year build of $494 million plus $31 million plus $15 million less $35 million, or $505 million.

For the first nine months of 2026 the release reports adjusted operating return on equity of 17.3%, compared with 14.0% a year earlier, and GAAP return on equity of 15.7%, compared with 2.7%. The release does not give a full-year forecast, and nothing in these figures should be read as one.

Sales: a record in RILAs

Retail annuity sales rose 22% to $6.5 billion. The composition matters more than the total. RILA sales reached a record $3.0 billion, up 44% from $2.1 billion. A RILA is a registered annuity that links returns to a market index and offers a defined level of downside protection, with a cap on upside, and it has become one of the fastest-growing retirement products in the United States. Variable annuity sales were $2.8 billion, down 3%. Fixed and fixed index annuity sales were $796 million, up 79% from $444 million. Institutional sales were $755 million, down from $1.0 billion.

Jackson's chief executive, Don Cummings, pointed to the record retail annuity sales in the release. Within retail annuities, RILA and fixed product sales grew sharply while variable annuity sales were slightly lower.

Capital, cash and the balance sheet

Jackson National Life's statutory total adjusted capital was $5.9 billion, and its risk-based capital (RBC) ratio was 524%. The release says the ratio was lower than in the second quarter because new business raised the required capital, which is the normal cost of growing a business that carries guarantees. The company reported free capital generation of $281 million and holding company free cash flow of $275 million, which included a $325 million distribution from the insurance subsidiary. Holding company cash was about $1.4 billion, against a minimum buffer of $325 million.

Jackson returned $291 million to shareholders in the quarter, $230 million of share repurchases and $61 million of dividends, which the release describes as 39% more than a year earlier. The board also increased the share repurchase authorization by $1 billion.

Two book-value figures need careful reading. Common equity was $7.9 billion, or $117.72 per share, against $138.17 per share at December 31, 2025. Calculated here, that is a decline of about 15% over nine months. Adjusted book value, which removes the effects of accumulated other comprehensive income and the hedging-related items that move with markets, was $11.1 billion, or $164.47 per share, against $155.78. That is an increase of about 6%. The two measures point in different directions because the GAAP figure absorbs market-driven valuation changes that Jackson's hedging programme is built to offset economically. Investors and policyholders should look at both, and at the statutory capital figures, rather than treating either book value as the whole picture. PPM America assets under management were $101.8 billion, up 13%.

What the release does not say

The release is a company document, and its adjusted measures are the company's own definitions. It does not give a stock-price reaction, an analyst view or any commentary on regulation. The comparison of hedging results with the prior year is also presented in a way that is hard to reconcile between the narrative and the table, so this article quotes the current-quarter figure and does not rely on the prior-year hedging comparison. Readers who need the exact definitions, including what counts as a notable item, should read the full exhibit.

What it means for annuity buyers and investors

For buyers, the main point is the product shift. RILAs offer more protection than a plain variable annuity but less growth potential, The size of Jackson's RILA sales shows strong demand for this type of product, although the release does not explain why. A buyer should still compare caps, buffers or floors, surrender charges and the insurer's financial strength, since the guarantee is only as good as the company that issues it. Jackson's 524% RBC ratio and $5.9 billion of statutory capital are the type of figure to check.

For investors, the quarter shows how much GAAP earnings can move around in a business built on hedged guarantees, and why the company steers attention to adjusted operating earnings and capital generation. A buyback authorization raised by $1 billion also signals that management considers its capital position comfortable, although the release itself does not say how quickly the authorization will be used. Anyone relying on this article for a decision should read Jackson's own filing and consider speaking to a licensed adviser, since it summarises one quarter's reported numbers and is not a recommendation.
source_name: Jackson Financial Inc. (third-quarter 2026 earnings release, SEC Exhibit 99.1)
image_alt: Retirement planning documents and calculator representing annuity products (illustrative)
key_points: Net income attributable to common shareholders was $847 million, or $12.37 per diluted share, against $65 million, or $0.92, a year earlier; adjusted operating earnings were $517 million ($7.55 per diluted share) against $433 million ($6.16).

Retail annuity sales rose 22% to $6.5 billion, led by a record $3.0 billion of registered index-linked annuity (RILA) sales, up 44% from $2.1 billion, while variable annuity sales slipped 3% to $2.8 billion.
Retail Annuities pretax adjusted operating earnings were $638 million against $494 million, and the four segments together came to $612 million against $505 million.
Jackson returned $291 million to shareholders ($230 million of buybacks and $61 million of dividends), and the board raised the repurchase authorization by $1 billion.

Common equity fell to $7.9 billion ($117.72 per share) from $138.17 at year-end 2025, while adjusted book value per share rose to $164.47 from $155.78, a gap that reflects how Jackson's hedging and market-risk accounting works.
why_it_matters: Jackson is one of the largest sellers of variable and index-linked annuities in the United States, so its figures show where retirement savers are putting money and how an insurer that hedges market guarantees is doing. The quarter pairs record RILA demand with very large swings between GAAP and adjusted results, a reminder that annuity insurers' headline net income can say little about underlying earnings.

title: Fairfax Financial's Third-Quarter Net Earnings Fall to $1,097 Million as an $859 Million Investment Loss Offsets Higher Insurance Revenue and a Stronger Underwriting Result
summary: Fairfax Financial's interim report for the nine months to September 30, 2026 shows third-quarter net earnings of US$1,096.9 million against US$1,245.7 million, insurance revenue up about 6% to US$8.77 billion, and net losses on investments of US$858.7 million that cut total investment income from US$1.39 billion to US$188 million.
description:
Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited, the Toronto-based insurance and reinsurance holding company, has published its interim report for the nine months ended September 30, 2026. The report was furnished to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Form 6-K, and all amounts below are in U.S. dollars, as the company reports. Differences and percentages that do not appear in the report are calculated here and labelled as such. This article uses the financial statement figures the report presents and does not cover measures such as the combined ratio, premiums written, book value per share or catastrophe losses, and nothing is inferred about them.

Net earnings

Third-quarter net earnings were US$1,096.9 million, compared with US$1,245.7 million in the third quarter of 2025, a decline of about 12% calculated here. Net earnings attributable to shareholders of Fairfax, after the share belonging to minority holders in subsidiaries, were US$929.6 million against US$1,151.7 million, a decline of about 19%. Per diluted share that was US$43.32 against US$52.04, and per basic share US$46.45 against US$55.90.

For the nine months, net earnings were US$3,394.7 million against US$3,800.6 million, and net earnings attributable to shareholders were US$3,018.0 million against US$3,534.1 million. Diluted earnings per share for the nine months were US$137.65 against US$156.31, and basic earnings per share US$147.60 against US$168.31. Pre-tax earnings were US$1,425.8 million for the quarter against US$1,564.6 million, and US$4,428.4 million for the nine months against US$4,684.3 million. The gap between pre-tax and net earnings in the quarter, calculated here, is US$328.9 million, which covers income taxes.

The insurance side improved

Insurance revenue, the line that shows the premiums earned for coverage provided in the period under the IFRS 17 accounting standard, rose to US$8,767.8 million from US$8,266.7 million, an increase of about 6% calculated here. For the nine months it was US$24,776.8 million against US$23,484.6 million, up about 5%.

The insurance service result, which is insurance revenue less the incurred cost of claims and expenses, was US$1,307.2 million against US$1,243.5 million for the quarter, up about 5%. For the nine months it was US$3,636.5 million against US$2,850.8 million, up about 28%. The net reinsurance result, which reflects the cost of the reinsurance Fairfax buys to protect itself, was a negative US$449.7 million in the quarter against a negative US$571.1 million, and negative US$1,041.3 million for the nine months against negative US$1,259.5 million. Combining these, the underwriting-related results were stronger over the nine months, although the report's income statement is not a substitute for the combined ratio and other metrics the company discusses in its management commentary.

The investment side fell

The third quarter's smaller profit comes from investments. Interest and dividends were US$668.7 million against US$655.4 million, and the share of profit of associates, companies in which Fairfax holds a significant but non-controlling stake, rose to US$378.0 million from US$305.0 million. Those two lines grew. But net gains and losses on investments, which capture changes in market value, swung to a net loss of US$858.7 million from a net gain of US$426.2 million. Adding the three lines gives total investment income and gains of US$188.0 million for the quarter against US$1,386.6 million a year earlier. The nine-month totals follow the same pattern: interest and dividends of US$2,068.0 million, associates' profit of US$792.3 million and net investment losses of US$475.7 million, for US$2,384.6 million in total against US$4,926.8 million in 2025, when net investment gains were US$2,434.3 million.

This is the central feature of Fairfax's accounts. The company runs a large investment portfolio, with cash and investments, net of derivative obligations, of US$77,255.0 million at September 30, 2026, against US$74,859.8 million at December 31, 2025. Interest and dividend income from that portfolio is steady and grew. The market-value line is volatile, and in one quarter it can add or remove hundreds of millions of dollars. The report does not break down in the figures used here which holdings produced the US$858.7 million loss, so this article does not attempt to.

Capital, cash and shareholder returns

Common shareholders' equity was US$26,911.8 million against US$26,282.6 million at year-end, about 2% higher calculated here, and total equity including non-controlling interests was US$31,996.1 million against US$30,874.1 million. Equity rose even though the company repurchased a large amount of stock.

Share repurchases are the notable capital-allocation move. In the first nine months of 2026 Fairfax bought 1,086,435 shares for US$1,771.8 million, against 541,794 shares for US$856.8 million in the same period of 2025. Calculated here, that is an average price of about US$1,631 per share, against about US$1,581 a year earlier. Within the nine months, buybacks were much lower in the third quarter, at US$51.2 million against US$495.9 million in the third quarter of 2025. Dividends were US$15.00 per share for the nine months, with none declared in the third quarter.

Cash and investments held at the holding company level, which are the funds available to the parent for debt service, buybacks and acquisitions, fell to US$1,935.3 million from US$2,724.9 million at the end of 2025, a decline of about 29% calculated here. The fall is consistent with the heavy repurchasing and dividend, but this article has no detail on what else moved.

A cash flow figure to watch

One figure stands out. Cash provided by operating activities was US$1,102.2 million in the third quarter against US$2,152.3 million, and only US$215.9 million for the nine months against US$3,718.0 million. Operating cash flow at an insurer can differ from earnings for timing reasons, so a low figure is not by itself a warning. This article does not have the explanation for the difference, and readers should look at the cash flow statement notes and the management's discussion for the reasons.

Other disclosures

The report states that the Middle East conflict had no significant impacts on the company's financial condition at the time of writing. It also records that the option to purchase the remaining minority interest in Allied World, one of Fairfax's insurance subsidiaries, has been extended to December 31, 2029.

What this means

For policyholders of Fairfax's subsidiaries, the most relevant fact is that insurance revenue and the insurance service result both grew, and equity increased. For shareholders, the quarter shows both the strength and the volatility of Fairfax's model: steady underwriting and interest income, with an investment line that can overwhelm both in a single quarter. None of this is a forecast, and the interim report is the company's own document, not an independent assessment. Anyone making a financial decision should read the full report and consult a licensed adviser.
source_name: Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited (third-quarter 2026 interim report, Form 6-K filed with the SEC)
image_alt: Financial reports and charts representing an insurance and investment holding company (illustrative)
key_points: Third-quarter net earnings were US$1,096.9 million against US$1,245.7 million a year earlier; net earnings attributable to shareholders were US$929.6 million against US$1,151.7 million, or US$43.32 per diluted share against US$52.04.
Insurance revenue rose to US$8,767.8 million from US$8,266.7 million, and the insurance service result improved to US$1,307.2 million from US$1,243.5 million.
Net losses on investments of US$858.7 million, against gains of US$426.2 million a year earlier, cut total investment income and gains to US$188.0 million from US$1,386.6 million.

Cash and investments held at the holding company fell to US$1,935.3 million from US$2,724.9 million at year-end 2025, after nine-month share repurchases of US$1,771.8 million, roughly double the US$856.8 million of the same period in 2025.
Nine-month operating cash flow was only US$215.9 million against US$3,718.0 million, a large gap that the figures alone do not explain.
why_it_matters: Fairfax is Canada's best-known insurance-and-investment holding company, and its results show how much an insurer's reported profit can depend on investment marks rather than underwriting. In this quarter the insurance operations improved while investment valuation losses pulled earnings down, which is the opposite of the pattern seen a year ago.

title: A Magnitude 4.9 Earthquake Off South Australia Shook Adelaide: What Australian Home Insurance Covers and Why Earthquake Deductibles and Aftershock Clauses Matter
summary: A magnitude 4.9 earthquake about 100 kilometres offshore shook Adelaide and much of South Australia on October 27, 2026, with no damage or injuries reported at the time, prompting a look at how standard Australian home and contents policies treat earthquake damage and what history says about the state's seismic risk.
description:
At 7:48am local time on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, an earthquake of magnitude 4.9 was recorded by Geoscience Australia off the coast of South Australia. The agency placed it about 10 kilometres below the surface and roughly 100 kilometres offshore, between Kangaroo Island and the state's south-east coast. Insurance Business Australia reported that about 700 felt reports arrived within an hour, spread from Gawler north of Adelaide to Beachport in the south-east and inland to Naracoorte. At the time of that report no damage or injuries had been reported, and seismologist Jonathan Bathgate called it a significant earthquake, warned that aftershocks were possible and said there was no tsunami threat. This article explains what the event means for people who own or insure property in Australia. It uses only what was reported at the time, so it does not describe any later damage or claims.

How big is a magnitude 4.9?

Magnitude is measured on a logarithmic scale, so a magnitude 5 earthquake releases far more energy than a magnitude 4. A 4.9 is moderate: widely felt, often capable of rattling objects and cracking weak plaster or chimneys close to the source, but not usually causing severe structural damage when it is 100 kilometres away and 10 kilometres deep. That is consistent with the reports of no damage. Geoscience Australia records around 100 earthquakes of magnitude 3 or more in Australia each year, so tremors are not unusual in Australia. One such event does not show that Adelaide has become more active.

What history says about South Australia

South Australia has experienced larger earthquakes. The 1954 Adelaide earthquake, of about magnitude 5.4, produced more than 30,000 claims, according to the history the article cites, with losses recorded at about £3 million at the time. A 2022 Geoscience Australia review suggests the 1954 event may have been larger than first estimated. The 1897 Beachport earthquake, of magnitude 6.5, is the largest documented in the state. These events show that a moderate quake close to a population centre can create widespread claims for cracked walls, damaged chimneys and broken contents, even when no one is killed.

Elsewhere in Australia, the 1989 Newcastle earthquake had insured losses that the Insurance Council of Australia put at $862 million at the time, which on a normalised basis made it the third costliest insured catastrophe in the country. The 2021 Victorian earthquake, of magnitude 5.9, produced about 1,700 claims in its first days. Together they show a pattern: large numbers of small to moderate claims rather than total destruction.

What a standard policy covers

According to the article, earthquake damage is generally covered under standard Australian home and contents insurance policies. Policy wording still varies, so the safe course is to read your product disclosure statement rather than assume.

Three features are worth checking.

First, the excess, which is the amount a policyholder pays on each claim. Some policies apply a different or higher excess to certain events. The article's broker advice is to check earthquake deductibles specifically.

Second, sub-limits, which cap what an insurer pays for certain types of loss, such as damage to fences, retaining walls, outbuildings or swimming pools. These items are often most exposed in a tremor and may be covered for less than the main building.

Third, the way a policy treats aftershocks. Earthquakes are commonly followed by smaller tremors. If a policy defines an event by a time window, such as all shocks within 72 hours counting as one earthquake, then a single deductible applies; if each aftershock counts separately, a policyholder could face several excesses. The article tells brokers and policyholders to check how aftershocks are grouped. The 72-hour window is an illustration of how such clauses can work, not a statement about any particular policy.

The portfolio view

Insurers think about earthquake as a low-frequency risk that can produce a large single-event loss. The article notes a view from Moody's that earthquake has become the bigger national portfolio concern for insurers now that the government's cyclone reinsurance pool absorbs a large part of cyclone risk. That is an assessment about portfolios, not a prediction that an earthquake is imminent.

In scale terms, the Insurance Council of Australia's tally for the 2025–26 catastrophe season was 147,552 claims and $3.98 billion in insured losses, according to the article. That total comes mostly from storms, floods and cyclones, which shows how frequent weather catastrophes dominate annual losses. Earthquakes are rarer, which is why a single event can surprise an insurer's accumulation models. The article also cites Aon commentary after the magnitude 8.8 Kamchatka earthquake in 2025, saying insurers are likely to revisit earthquake and tsunami sub-limits, which suggests the market is paying attention to this peril.

What homeowners can do

There is no need for alarm after a magnitude 4.9 tremor with no reported damage, but it is a good time for practical steps.

Check the policy. Find the sections on earthquake, the excess, any sub-limits and how multiple shocks are treated.

Check the sum insured. Underinsurance is a common problem after any catastrophe, and rebuilding costs have risen. Use your insurer's calculator or a quantity surveyor's estimate.

Look around the property. After any tremor, inspect for new cracks in walls, ceilings and foundations, and for loose chimneys or tiles. Photograph any damage before repairs, and keep receipts for emergency work. If you find damage, contact your insurer promptly, since policies set their own notice requirements.

Do not assume damage is from the quake. Insurers may distinguish between new damage and existing settlement cracks, so dated photos of the property before an event can be useful evidence.

Limits of this article

This article is based on one trade-press report and the official earthquake details it cites. It does not contain claims data from any insurer, and it does not forecast further tremors. Geoscience Australia and the South Australian State Emergency Service publish current information after seismic events, and your insurer's website and product disclosure statement are the authority on your own cover. It is general information, not personal advice.
source_name: Insurance Business Australia (reporting Geoscience Australia and insurance commentary)
image_alt: City buildings and street representing an Australian capital after a tremor (illustrative)
key_points: Geoscience Australia recorded a magnitude 4.9 earthquake at 7:48am local time on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, about 10 kilometres deep and roughly 100 kilometres offshore between Kangaroo Island and the south-east coast of South Australia.

About 700 felt reports came in within an hour, from Gawler to Beachport and inland to Naracoorte; no damage or injuries had been reported when the article was written, and there was no tsunami threat.

Earthquake damage is generally covered under standard Australian home and contents policies, but deductibles, sub-limits and how a policy groups aftershocks into one event can change what a policyholder recovers.

The 1954 Adelaide earthquake, of about magnitude 5.4, produced more than 30,000 claims, and the 1989 Newcastle earthquake caused insured losses of $862 million at the time, showing that moderate quakes near cities can be costly.
A quake of this size does not by itself mean Adelaide is becoming more seismically active; Geoscience Australia records around 100 earthquakes of magnitude 3 or more in Australia each year.
why_it_matters: Most Australians think of cyclones, floods and bushfires when they think of catastrophe cover, but earthquakes are also included in standard home policies and are a real exposure for insurers and homeowners. A moderate offshore tremor is a low-cost prompt to check what your policy says before it matters.

title: SBI Life's First-Half FY27 Profit Rises 17% to Rs 1,270 Crore and Value of New Business Climbs 19% to Rs 3,270 Crore, While Costs Take a Larger Share of Premium
summary: SBI Life Insurance reported profit after tax up 17% to Rs 1,270 crore for the half year ended September 30, 2026, value of new business up 19% to Rs 3,270 crore, gross written premium up 13% to Rs 48,400 crore and a solvency ratio of 1.97, while its total cost ratio rose to 11.7% from 10.9%.
description:
SBI Life Insurance Company, the listed life insurer promoted by State Bank of India, has reported results for the half year ended September 30, 2026, the first half of fiscal 2027. This article uses a report of those results by Kotak Neo. The report gives half-year figures only, so quarter-only numbers are not covered here, and other websites have published different quarter-only figures that this article did not use. Differences, percentages and rounding checks that do not appear in the source are calculated here and labelled. All amounts are in Indian rupees; one crore is ten million, and one lakh crore is one trillion.

Profit and returns

Profit after tax rose 17% to Rs 1,270 crore. The source does not give the prior-year figure, but a 17% rise implies roughly Rs 1,085 crore a year earlier, calculated here. Return on equity was 12.9%, against 12.3% in the same period last year. Net worth, the shareholders' funds on the balance sheet, rose 12% to Rs 20,530 crore.

For a life insurer, profit after tax is a lagging indicator, because the accounting profit recognised in a year depends on policies sold over many years. The measure the industry watches for new business is the value of new business, or VNB, which is the estimated present value of future profits from policies sold in the period.

Value of new business

VNB grew 19% to Rs 3,270 crore, from Rs 2,750 crore. The VNB margin, which divides VNB by the annualised premium equivalent, or APE, was reported at 27.9%, against 27.8% a year earlier. APE is a standardised measure that counts regular premiums in full and single premiums at one-tenth of their value, so that different product mixes can be compared. APE rose 18% to Rs 11,750 crore.

There is a small discrepancy to flag. Dividing Rs 3,270 crore by Rs 11,750 crore gives 27.8%, calculated here, not the 27.9% the report states. The gap may be due to rounding in the underlying figures, which are shown to the nearest Rs 10 crore, and it does not change the picture: margins were roughly flat, so VNB grew mainly because the volume of business grew. That is a healthy pattern for a growing insurer, but it also means profitability per rupee of new business did not noticeably improve.

Premium growth

Gross written premium, which includes new business and renewals, rose 13% to Rs 48,400 crore, from Rs 42,900 crore. New business premium grew 10% to Rs 20,260 crore, from Rs 18,350 crore. Renewal premium, which is the money from existing policyholders paying again, grew 15% to Rs 28,150 crore, from Rs 24,550 crore. The two components add to Rs 48,410 crore, calculated here, which differs from the headline by Rs 10 crore because of rounding in the source.

Renewal premium rising faster than new business is typically a sign of a book that is maturing and policyholders continuing to pay, although the source does not provide persistency ratios, which measure how many policies stay in force. Without them, this article cannot say how well customers are keeping their policies.

Individual business, which covers policies sold to individuals rather than groups, grew faster than the total in the new business line. Individual new business premium rose 13% to Rs 13,730 crore, and individual rated premium, rose 12% to Rs 9,720 crore. SBI Life reported a private-market share of 22.6% by individual rated premium and 25.2% by individual new business premium.

Embedded value and assets

Indian embedded value, a measure of the value of the company's net assets plus the present value of profits from its in-force business, rose 15% to Rs 87,350 crore, from Rs 76,000 crore. Assets under management grew to Rs 5.27 lakh crore from Rs 4.81 lakh crore. The source describes this as growth of 9%, but the two figures give about 9.6%, calculated here, so the percentage is likely rounded down or the underlying amounts are rounded.

Solvency and investment quality

The solvency ratio was 1.97, against a regulatory requirement of 1.50. Solvency is the ratio of available capital to required capital, so 1.97 means the insurer holds about 1.3 times the minimum, calculated here as 1.97 divided by 1.50. The source says about 94% of the debt investments are rated AAA or are sovereign securities, which indicates a conservative credit profile on that portion of the portfolio. It does not describe the equity portfolio.

Costs rose

The least flattering numbers are on costs. The total cost ratio, which compares expenses and commissions to premium, rose to 11.7% from 10.9%. The operating expense ratio rose to 6.9% from 6.2%, and the commission ratio edged up to 4.8% from 4.7%. Those components add up to the total in both periods: 6.9 plus 4.8 is 11.7, and 6.2 plus 4.7 is 10.9.

In other words, almost all the increase came from operating expenses rather than commission. The source does not say why. This article does not know the cause and does not guess at one. What the numbers show is that expenses grew faster than premium, which pulled on margins even as VNB grew.

Management and market reaction

The source paraphrases chief executive Amit Jhingran as pointing to the growth and the strength of the company's distribution. The article does not provide a direct quote. SBI Life's shares closed at Rs 1,633 on the National Stock Exchange on October 27, 2026, according to the source. This article does not describe how the stock moved after the results.

What the results do not tell us

The report gives no persistency data, no guidance for the second half, no product-level breakdown of protection against savings policies, and no comparison to rivals' margins. Without those, the results show a growing, well-capitalised insurer, but not how sustainable its margins are. Policyholders should look at the claim settlement ratio and persistency figures in the company's public disclosures, and investors should read the full results filed with the exchanges. This article is a summary of one secondary report, general information and not investment advice.
source_name: Kotak Neo (report on SBI Life Insurance's H1 FY27 results)

key_points: For the half year ended September 30, 2026, profit after tax rose 17% to Rs 1,270 crore, value of new business (VNB) rose 19% to Rs 3,270 crore from Rs 2,750 crore, and return on equity was 12.9% against 12.3%.

Gross written premium grew 13% to Rs 48,400 crore: new business premium rose 10% to Rs 20,260 crore and renewal premium rose 15% to Rs 28,150 crore; annualised premium equivalent (APE) rose 18% to Rs 11,750 crore.
Indian embedded value rose 15% to Rs 87,350 crore from Rs 76,000 crore, assets under management reached Rs 5.27 lakh crore, and the solvency ratio was 1.97 against the required 1.50.
Costs grew faster than premium: the total cost ratio rose to 11.7% from 10.9%, with the operating expense ratio at 6.9% against 6.2% and commissions at 4.8% against 4.7%.
The source states VNB margin as 27.9%, but dividing the reported VNB by APE gives 27.8%, and it gives half-year figures only, with no persistency data or guidance.
why_it_matters: SBI Life is one of India's largest private-sector life insurers, so its results are a gauge of how fast the country's life insurance market is growing and how profitable new policies are. Profit and VNB growth outpaced premium growth, but the rising expense ratio shows the cost of that growth, which matters to investors and policyholders alike.

title: FCA Tells Vertically Integrated General Insurance Groups to Evidence How They Manage Conflicts of Interest in Placement, Panels, Pay and Disclosure
summary: The Financial Conduct Authority's guidance on vertically integrated general insurance business models says firms combining underwriting, distribution and related services must identify, prevent or manage conflicts of interest, be able to evidence their controls on request, make clear and fair disclosures and keep group structures simple enough to supervise.
description:
The UK Financial Conduct Authority has published a guidance page for general insurance firms titled General insurance vertically integrated business models: managing conflicts of interest. The page's metadata shows 21 July 2026, while the page text says it was first published on 23 July 2026. This article uses the later date where it needs one and flags the difference. The guidance is addressed to firms in the general insurance market, which covers products such as motor, home, travel and commercial insurance rather than life insurance. It does not give a deadline, it does not contain statistics and it does not name a specific incident as the trigger; a past FCA fine against an insurance intermediary appears only as a link under further reading, and this article does not rely on it.

What a vertically integrated model is

In the FCA's description, a vertically integrated business model is one that combines several steps in the chain between a customer and an insurance policy. Those steps can include underwriting, which is taking on the risk, distribution, which is selling the policy, intermediary activity such as broking, premium finance, which lets customers pay in instalments, and ancillary services. A group may own an insurer and a broker, or a broker may be financed by or invest in an insurer. The FCA notes that ownership, investment or financing links between entities create the potential for conflicts of interest.

The regulator is careful to say that a conflict is not automatically a reason to reject a model. The point is that when the same group has a financial interest on both sides of a decision, such as which insurer's product a broker recommends, it must have systems to stop that interest from working against the customer.

What the FCA expects

The page sets out a series of expectations. Firms are expected to identify conflicts and then prevent or manage them. They should review their business models, governance, systems and controls, and they should be able to show evidence if the FCA asks. The areas where the FCA says it may ask for evidence are:

placement decisions, panel design and product recommendations, meaning how a firm chooses which insurers to approach and which products to put in front of a customer;

customer communications;

remuneration and incentives, including how staff and the firm are paid;

how responsibilities are allocated across the legal entities in a group;

product governance and fair value, meaning how the product is designed and whether it gives customers fair value;

management information and the oversight senior managers exercise.

Firms are also expected to assess the risk when something changes, such as new ownership, new investments, debt financing or intragroup arrangements, and to notify the FCA promptly of material changes.

Disclosure, independence and the limits of disclosure

The FCA expects disclosures to be clear, fair and not misleading. It adds two points that matter in practice. A firm that presents itself as independent must make that description match how it actually operates. And disclosure is not enough: telling customers about a conflict does not replace managing it. In other words, a disclosure statement is not a substitute for controls.

This ties in with the FCA's Consumer Duty, which requires firms to deliver good outcomes to retail customers. The page lists the relevant parts of the FCA Handbook as the Principles for Businesses (PRIN), the systems and controls rules on conflicts (SYSC 10), SYSC 19.2F, the product governance rules (PROD 4), the Consumer Duty and the threshold condition COND 2.3.1A.

Structure and supervision

Another expectation concerns group structure. The FCA says firms must confirm that their group structures allow effective supervision, citing COND 2.3.1A, which is part of the minimum conditions a firm must meet to be authorised. It says overly complex models should be simplified. The practical meaning is that a regulator needs to be able to see which entity does what and who is accountable, and a web of linked companies can make that difficult.

The FCA says it will take supervisory or enforcement action where behaviour may harm consumers, weaken competition or obscure accountability. The page does not say what that action would be, and it does not set out a timetable or a list of firms.

What it means for different readers

For insurance groups and brokers, the page is a checklist of the evidence the FCA may ask for. Firms that own both an insurer and a distributor will want to look at whether panel decisions can be explained on customer-outcome grounds, whether incentives reward steering and whether independence claims are accurate. Firms undergoing a change of ownership or financing should consider the notification expectation.

For customers, the guidance does not change anything immediately, and the page does not create new rights. But it gives a benchmark. If a broker describes itself as independent, the FCA says that description must be accurate. Customers can ask a broker who owns it, how many insurers it approaches and how it is paid, and can complain to the firm and then to the Financial Ombudsman Service if they believe they were treated unfairly. The question list is general consumer advice and not part of the FCA page.

What we do not know

The page is guidance and expectations rather than new rules, and it does not say how many firms it affects or whether the FCA plans a review. It also does not describe how firms should prove compliance in detail. Law-firm notes on the guidance exist and may add interpretation, but this article relies on the FCA's own page. Readers who work in the sector should read the full guidance and the Handbook provisions it cites. This article is general information and not legal advice.
source_name: Financial Conduct Authority (guidance page: General insurance vertically integrated business models: managing conflicts of interest)
image_alt: Office meeting table representing insurance governance and oversight (illustrative)
key_points: The FCA's page describes vertically integrated models as those that can combine underwriting, distribution, intermediary activity, premium finance and ancillary services, and says ownership, investment or financing links between entities can create potential conflicts.

The FCA says a conflict does not automatically make a model unacceptable, but firms must identify, prevent or manage conflicts and be ready to show evidence on placement decisions, panel design, product recommendations, remuneration and incentives, product governance and management information.
Firms that present themselves as independent must make sure that description reflects how they actually operate, and disclosure alone is not enough to manage a conflict.
Group structures must allow effective supervision under threshold condition COND 2.3.1A, and the FCA expects overly complex models to be simplified and material changes to be notified promptly.
The page sets out expectations and no deadlines; the FCA says it will take supervisory or enforcement action where behaviour may harm consumers, weaken competition or obscure accountability.
why_it_matters: Many UK insurance customers buy through a broker or intermediary that is owned by, financed by or commercially tied to an insurer or another group company. The FCA's guidance sets out in one place what it expects such groups to be able to prove, which matters for anyone who relies on a broker's claim to be impartial.

title: Ontario's FSRA Warns Drivers That Some GAP Insurance Sold by Unlicensed Businesses May Not Pay Out, Including Products Marketed as 'Loyalty Programs'
summary: Ontario's financial regulator FSRA says it has found guaranteed asset protection (GAP) products sold by unlicensed businesses and individuals, some naming an insurer that never issued the policy and some marketed as loyalty programs, and warns that claims may not be honoured.
description:
The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario, known as FSRA, has issued a warning to drivers in the province about guaranteed asset protection insurance, usually called GAP insurance. The announcement as displayed on FSRA's site does not show a publication date, so this article does not give one. The warning's central message is that some GAP products on sale in Ontario are being sold by businesses and people who are not licensed to sell insurance, and that buyers of those products may not be protected.

What GAP insurance is

GAP insurance is an optional product that is commonly offered when someone buys or leases a vehicle with a loan or lease. A standard auto policy that covers theft or a total loss pays the actual cash value of the car at the time, meaning what it was worth on the day, after depreciation. New vehicles lose value quickly, so a driver can owe more on the loan than the car is worth. GAP cover is meant to pay the difference between the car's actual cash value and the balance still owed on the loan or lease if the car is stolen or written off.

FSRA gives an example. A driver owes $30,000 on a vehicle, and the vehicle is valued at $24,000 after it is declared a total loss. The auto insurer pays the $24,000, and the driver would still owe $6,000 to the lender. A valid GAP policy would pay that $6,000. Without it, the driver pays it out of pocket, even though the car is gone.

What FSRA found

FSRA reports that it found GAP products being sold by unlicensed businesses and individuals. It describes several problems.

Some of the products name an insurer, which can make them look legitimate, even though no licensed insurer actually issued the policy. A buyer who reads a certificate with an insurer's name on it may reasonably think the cover is real.

Some are marketed as loyalty programs. In one version, a business offers to credit an amount toward the purchase of another vehicle if the first one is written off or stolen. FSRA says that a product that promises this type of payment is still insurance under Ontario's Insurance Act, no matter what it is called. Calling it a loyalty program does not remove the need for a licence.

FSRA says insurance in Ontario can be sold only by licensed insurers, agents or brokers. If the seller is not licensed, the regulator warns, buyers may have paid hundreds of dollars for policies that may not be valid. Jordan Solway, FSRA's Executive Vice President for property and casualty insurance, is quoted saying that claims may not be honoured. This article does not know how many drivers are affected, how many sellers were identified or whether any have been named, because the announcement does not give that information.

How to check before you buy

FSRA's guidance to consumers is practical. Before buying GAP cover, a driver should:

confirm which licensed insurer is providing the cover;

check that the seller and insurer are licensed, using FSRA's licence verification tools;

make sure a licensed agent or broker is involved in the sale;

read the contract, including what counts as a covered loss and what is excluded; and

ask how the claims process works and who pays.

These steps also apply to people who have already bought GAP cover. A driver who is unsure should find the name of the insurer on the paperwork, contact that insurer directly using contact details found independently, and ask FSRA whether the seller is licensed.

What FSRA says it will do

FSRA says it will continue to monitor the market and take action against violations. People who have concerns or want to file a complaint can contact FSRA, whose consumer line is 1-800-668-0128.

What we cannot say

The FSRA announcement does not say how many drivers bought the products, how much money is involved beyond the figure of hundreds of dollars per policy, or which businesses are involved. It does not say whether buyers can recover their money. A driver who thinks they bought an invalid policy could ask the seller for a refund, tell their lender and contact FSRA or a licensed broker; these are general suggestions rather than steps FSRA's page prescribes.

Why the warning matters beyond Ontario

The underlying risk is not unique to one province. Any product that promises to pay money after a loss is insurance in substance, and the protections that come with a licence, including regulatory oversight and a route to complain, only apply if the seller is actually licensed. For a driver, the cost of checking is a few minutes before signing. The cost of not checking, if the policy proves worthless, could be thousands of dollars owed on a vehicle that no longer exists. This article is general information, not legal advice.
source_name: Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA warning announcement)

key_points: GAP insurance is optional cover, often sold at dealerships, that pays the difference between a vehicle's actual cash value and the remaining loan or lease balance if the car is stolen or written off.
FSRA's example: if a driver owes $30,000 and the car is valued at $24,000 after a total loss, the $6,000 shortfall is the gap that GAP cover is meant to pay.

FSRA found GAP products sold by unlicensed businesses and individuals; some name an insurer even though no licensed insurer issued the policy, and some are described as 'loyalty programs' that credit toward another vehicle, which FSRA says is still insurance under the Insurance Act.

If the seller is unlicensed, a buyer could discover only after a total loss that the policy does not pay, leaving them owing a loan balance on a car they no longer have.
